extracted.intended_audience: prospective peer reviewers (clinicians/researchers) preparing to review scientific/medical manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for prospective peer reviewers on deciding whether to accept review invitations, systematically assessing each manuscript section, and writing constructive, confidential reviews for scientific/medical journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding whether to accept a review invitation
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering a peer review opportunity, ask: (1) Do I have sufficient expertise in the area of interest? (2) Can I complete the peer review in the allotted time? (3) Do I have any ethical conflicts of interest?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot meet deadlines, notify editors immediately and decline. The earlier editors are informed, the sooner they can find alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer role and primary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of peer reviewers is to provide insightful commentary and suggestions to the editor, drawing on familiarity of the field and assessment of the manuscript; the primary skill is the ability to critically read scientific literature and recognize both positive and negative traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prospective reviewers may not need exceptional expertise; with core subject knowledge, critical reading and reviewing skills can be cultivated through experience and mentored review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical expertise and use of statistics editors
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not unusual to feel intimidated by statistical methods; expertise in statistics is not a requirement for reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many journals have a statistics editor—reviewers may suggest or request additional review by the statistics editor when preparing a peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical conflicts, confidentiality, and appropriateness to review
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess ethical requirements: manuscripts should not directly compete with a reviewer's own research; avoid reviewing for authors with close personal or professional relationships; unpublished manuscripts are confidential and should not be shared or integrated into a reviewer's work prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow guidelines from publication ethics committees (e.g., COPE, ICMJE). Decline if conflicts exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Delays are a major hurdle. Reviewers must be able to meet the journal's deadlines for responding to invitations and for submitting reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unable to meet deadlines, notify editors immediately and decline so editors can find alternative reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step reading approach
rubrics_metrics.description: First, read the manuscript in full with a broad outlook to assess novelty and major fatal flaws; second, perform a detailed assessment systematically evaluating each section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A brief literature search at the first stage may help contextualize the submission and assess novelty. During the second read, systematically evaluate each section (see section-specific guidelines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking specific concerns with locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific concerns should be clearly noted with line numbers or paragraph locations so that the authors can easily address them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes revisions more efficient and precise for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit grammar and style comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are recommended to limit commentary regarding grammar or style as these tasks are better served by the journal's copy editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus reviewer effort on scientific validity, methods, interpretation, and clarity of argument rather than copyediting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title — clarity and conveyance of research question
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the title clearly convey the research question and content?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend revisions if the title is ambiguous or fails to represent scope or question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract — concision, methods, results alignment, and not overstating
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the abstract concise and brief? Do the abstract methods include enough information to generally interpret the study's results? Do the abstract results align with the study's reported findings? Do the abstract conclusions align with the study's conclusions? Does the abstract avoid overstating the importance of the study?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check consistency between abstract and manuscript; request edits if methods/results/conclusions are misaligned or overstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction — clarity, context, and presentation of question/objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the introduction clear and focused? Is sufficient context provided to understand the rationale for the study? Does the introduction clearly present the study's research question, objective, and scope?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend adding background or clarifying scope if rationale or objectives are vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods — reproducibility, statistical appropriateness, and ethics compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Is enough methodological detail provided to replicate the study? Are the statistical analyses appropriate and understandable? Do the reported statistics require review by the statistics editor? Does the study comply with ethical standards (e.g., informed patient consent, IRB approval)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag missing details that prevent replication; request ethics documentation or statistical review as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results — relevance to research question and clarity of figures/tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the reported results address the research question and objective? Are any included tables and figures appropriately referenced within the text? Are table or figure legends clear and understandable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request reorganization or clarification if results do not directly address objectives or if figures/tables are unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion — interpretation and acknowledgment of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results appropriately interpreted and contextualized within the existing knowledge of the topic? Are the limitations of the study appropriately stated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag over-interpretation, missing comparisons to prior work, or insufficient discussion of limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion — alignment and avoidance of overstatement or unsupported claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the conclusion align with the research question stated in the introduction? Does the conclusion avoid overstating the importance of the results? Does the conclusion avoid expressing opinions and unsupported claims?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors to temper claims or better tie conclusions to presented evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: References — self-citation, accuracy, and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Is self-citation maintained at a reasonable amount? Are cited sources interpreted accurately? Are important and relevant references missing from citations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest adding missing key citations or correcting misinterpretations; flag excessive self-citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review structure: summary, major concerns, minor concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective review begins with a concise summary of the manuscript and brief assessment of novelty/significance, followed by major issues (methodological limitations, ethical concerns, questions about contribution), then minor points to improve clarity/readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Reviewer Evaluation Outline: Summary (impression, study type, importance), Major Concerns (prioritized key points and validity-affecting issues), Minor Concerns (unclear sentences, reference errors, figure/table labeling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Major concerns examples (validity-affecting issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: List any concerns that affect the validity of the paper such as inadequate research design, insufficient evidence to support the conclusion, ethical issues (confidentiality, anonymity, consent), or lack of novelty or meaningful contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize key points most important for authors and editors; provide specific advice to address these concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor concerns examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor concerns include unclear or ambiguous sentences, reference errors, suggestions for better labeling of figures, tables, or sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List these after major concerns; they are lower priority but improve readability and usability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments to authors — constructive, specific, avoid editorializing
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specific advice to address major concerns and avoid editorializing beyond the scope of a peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame feedback respectfully and constructively since comments are generally shared with authors verbatim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments to editor — confidential recommendation and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide recommendations on publication and a specific rationale for your publication recommendation in the confidential comments to the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations about acceptance or rejection should not appear in the portion of the review shared with authors; the confidential comments to the editor are the appropriate place for overall recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and collegiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should be constructive and adopt a collegial tone; peer review is not intended as an obstacle to publication but to enhance quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since reviewer comments are shared verbatim, frame feedback in a respectful manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional benefits and practice for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Serving as a peer reviewer offers professional benefits: exposure to study designs/statistics, strengthening critical appraisal skills, staying abreast of research, connecting with editors/experts, and fostering academic recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular practice and mentored reviewing help develop proficiency; consider these motivations when deciding to accept reviews.
